## 1. The raw file (`data/mturk_raw.csv`)

**Shape:** 12,838 rows × 10 columns. The paper also says 12,838 workers started the task, so this matches the authors' raw sample.

## 2. The notes against the data, paper and registration

**Sources:**
- **Paper:** the NBER working paper w22193, downloaded and read in full. I didn't get the published REStud version.
- **Registration:** the AEA registry page AEARCTR-0000714. I only saw it through a summarising fetch tool, but the exclusion rules it gave match what the paper quotes word for word from the registration.

### Treatment code table: partly checked, and one entry is wrong
The paper and registration list the arms in words, not as codes like "1.1". I couldn't find the replication package online, so the code-to-arm mapping isn't confirmed from the authors' files. Instead I checked it against how each code actually paid out.

**Confirmed by the payouts:**
- **1.3:** payout always 0.
- **1.1, 1.4, 1.2:** payout is exactly whole hundreds of points × 1¢, 4¢ and 10¢.
- **2:** whole thousands of points × 1¢.
- **5.1 / 5.2:** 40¢ if 2,000 points or more, otherwise 0.
- **5.3:** the same at 80¢.
- **6.1:** about 1% of workers got large payouts ($16–$28).
- **6.2:** about half got 2¢ per 100 points, the rest 0.

**Wrong:** code 10 (gift exchange) paid a flat **$0.40** to all 589 workers who have a payout. The paper ("a bonus of 40 cents") and the registration agree. The notes' "unexpected $1 bonus" is incorrect.

**Can't be told apart from the data:**
- 1.1 vs 3.1 vs 4.1 vs 4.2: all pay 1¢ per 100. The Red Cross arms record the payout as if paid to the worker.
- 1.2 vs 3.2: both 10¢ per 100.
- 5.1 (gain) vs 5.2 (loss): identical payouts.
- 1.3 vs 7 vs 8 vs 9: all pay nothing.

For those groups the labels rest on the notes alone.

### "16 arms, ~550 each": wrong count, right size
- **Arms:** the paper, the registration and the data all have **18** arms. The notes' own intro also says 18. (The registration text once says "seventeen", but it lists 18.)
- **Size:** "about 550 per treatment" is the paper's figure after cleaning (final N = 9,861). Raw counts are about 680–695 per code, so ~550 only holds after exclusions.

### The 3,500-point rule: misstated
The registration excludes subjects who **"score 4000 or more points"**. The 3,500 figure is only the reason given: the pilot showed scoring above 3,500 by hand is "physically impossible", so those subjects are probably using bots. The paper says it dropped 48 workers "above 4,000". In this file the two cutoffs differ: 65 rows are above 3,500 versus 50 above 4,000.

## 3. Other things the paper says that matter for cleaning
- **Registered exclusions:** the paper lists three:
  - not completing within 30 minutes (1,543 dropped);
  - re-entering as a new subject (364 dropped);

- **Exclusions added after registration:**
  - 721 workers lost to a Qualtrics server glitch that broke the score counter;
  - 187 workers whose work wasn't approved;

- **Can't identify the glitch rows:** there's no flag in this file, and the paper gives no time window. I can't reproduce that exclusion without the replication package.
- **Other errors in the notes:**
  - The task lasted **10 minutes**, not 15.
  - Arm 9, "task significance", actually reads "We are interested in how fast people choose to press digits and we would like you to do your very best." That's a weak match for Grant's idea of task significance, which matters for how you frame H2.
  - Gneezy & Rustichini, QJE 115(3), was published in **2000**, not 2001.

- The authors' own code-to-arm mapping, from the replication files.
- Which rows were hit by the Qualtrics glitch.
- The published REStud text, as opposed to the NBER working paper.

**§1 Introduction, p. 1 (PDF p. 3):**
> "The task for the subjects is to alternately press the "a" and "b" buttons on their keyboards as quickly as possible for ten minutes."

**§3.1, p. 13 (PDF p. 15), quoting the instructions workers saw:**
> "The object of this task is to alternately press the 'a' and 'b' buttons on your keyboard as quickly as possible for 10 minutes."

## (b) Gift exchange bonus (40 cents, not $1)

**§2 Treatments and Model, p. 8 (PDF p. 10):**
> "The final social preference treatment is a gift exchange treatment modelled upon Gneezy and List (2009): "In appreciation to you for performing this task, you will be paid a bonus of 40 cents. Your score will not affect your payment in any way." In this treatment there is no piece rate"

**§4.1 Average Effort, p. 18 (PDF p. 20):**

## (c) Task significance instructions

**§2, p. 11 (PDF p. 13):**
> "The final manipulation is based on the influential literature in psychology on task significance (Grant, 2008): workers work harder when they are informed about the significance of their job. Within our setting, we inform people that "Your score will not affect your payment in any way. We are interested in how fast people choose to press digits and we would like you to do your very best. So please try as hard as you can.""

**§3.1, p. 14 (PDF p. 16), the registered rules:**
> "We also pre-specified the roles for inclusion in the sample. > "The initial sample consists of 12,838 MTurk workers who started our experimental task. This sample exclusion, which we could not have anticipated, does not appear in the registration."

**pp. 14–15 (PDF pp. 16–17), the 48, 1,543 and 364 drops:**
> "We then applied the three specified sample restrictions. We dropped (i) 48 workers for scoring above 4,000 points, (ii) 1,543 workers for failing to complete the experiment (for example, many participants only filled out the demographics portion of the experiment and were never assigned a treatment), and (iii) 364 workers for stopping the task and logging in again. >
> "Summary Statistics. The final sample includes 9,861 subjects, about 550 per treatment."

**Footnote 14, p. 15:**
> "The two additional restrictions, which are immaterial for the results, were added before we analyzed the full data and were included in the pre-registration for the survey protocol AEARCTR-0000731 (see below)."

## How I put each rule into practice
1. **Score of 4,000 or more:** `buttonpresses >= 4000`. Rows with no score aren't dropped at this step. Nobody scored exactly 4,000, so "4,000 or more" and the paper's "above 4,000" drop the same people.
2. **Not finished within 30 minutes:** `finished == 0`, or more than 30 minutes between start and end time. That's 1,946 unfinished rows plus 74 finished ones that took longer than 30 minutes.
3. **Re-entrants:** every row whose ID appears more than once in the **raw** file. I flagged these before any other rule ran, so someone whose first try was dropped for another reason still counts as a re-entrant.
   - This step drops only 176 because 314 of the 490 rows were already gone after steps 1–2.
   - The 232 rows with no ID can't be matched to anyone, so they aren't flagged. All of them get dropped later by other rules anyway.
4. **Not approved:** `approved == 0`.
5. **Zero presses:** points missing **or** 0. The file has no zeros, so this step only drops rows with no score recorded. I based this on the paper saying these participants' "results were not recorded". It's the main judgment call here: if you want only literal zeros, this step drops nothing.

"""Stage 3: the analysis in preregistration.md.

One OLS of points on indicators for all 18 arms (reference 1.3, no covariates),
HC1 standard errors. Comparisons with 1.3 are t-tests on a coefficient; comparisons
between two other arms are Wald tests of equal coefficients (one restriction, so
the same as a t-test on the difference). All two-sided. Holm within each family.

Samples: primary (data/clean.csv), complete cases (no missing buttonpresses,
treatment or practicecount), and trimmed (also drop scores above 3,500).

Writes output/arm_stats.csv, output/tests.csv and output/fig_arm_means.png.
"""

from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
CLEAN = ROOT / "data" / "clean.csv"
OUT = ROOT / "output"

REF = "1.3"
ALPHA = 0.05

# (family, arm A, arm B): estimate is mean(A) - mean(B).
TESTS = [
    ("H1", "1.1", "1.3"),
    ("H1", "1.4", "1.3"),
    ("H1", "1.2", "1.3"),
    ("H1", "2", "1.3"),
    ("H1", "1.2", "1.4"),
    ("H1", "1.4", "1.1"),
    ("H2 primary", "7", "1.3"),
    ("H2 primary", "8", "1.3"),
    ("H2 primary", "9", "1.3"),
    ("H2 primary", "7", "2"),
    ("H2 primary", "8", "2"),
    ("H2 primary", "9", "2"),
    ("H2 secondary", "7", "1.1"),
    ("H2 secondary", "8", "1.1"),
    ("H2 secondary", "9", "1.1"),
    ("H3", "10", "1.3"),
]
FAMILY_SIZES = {"H1": 6, "H2 primary": 6, "H2 secondary": 3, "H3": 1}

H2_ARMS = ["7", "8", "9"]
SMALLEST_RATE = "2"


def load():
    df = pd.read_csv(CLEAN, dtype={"treatment": str})
    arms = pd.read_csv(OUT / "arm_counts.csv", dtype={"treatment": str})
    arms = arms[arms["treatment"] != "(missing)"].reset_index(drop=True)
    n = df["treatment"].value_counts()
    for t, expected in zip(arms["treatment"], arms["clean_n"]):
        assert n.get(t, 0) == expected, f"arm {t}: N {n.get(t, 0)} != arm_counts {expected}"
    assert len(df) == arms["clean_n"].sum(), "clean.csv rows != sum of arm_counts"
    assert set(n.index) == set(arms["treatment"]), "arm codes differ from arm_counts"
    return df, arms


def samples(df):
    complete = df.dropna(subset=["buttonpresses", "treatment", "practicecount"])
    trimmed = df[df["buttonpresses"] <= 3500]
    return {"primary": df, "complete_case": complete, "trimmed_3500": trimmed}


def fit(d, codes):
    others = [c for c in codes if c != REF]
    X = pd.DataFrame({c: (d["treatment"] == c).astype(float) for c in others}, index=d.index)
    X = sm.add_constant(X)
    res = sm.OLS(d["buttonpresses"].astype(float), X).fit(cov_type="HC1", use_t=True)
    return res, list(X.columns)


def run_tests(res, cols, sample):
    rows = []
    for family, a, b in TESTS:
        r = np.zeros(len(cols))
        if a != REF:
            r[cols.index(a)] += 1
        if b != REF:
            r[cols.index(b)] -= 1
        t = res.t_test(r)
        lo, hi = t.conf_int(alpha=ALPHA)[0]
        rows.append({
            "sample": sample, "family": family, "test": f"{a} vs {b}",
            "arm_a": a, "arm_b": b,
            "estimate": float(t.effect[0]), "se": float(t.sd[0][0]),
            "ci_low": lo, "ci_high": hi,
            "t": float(t.tvalue[0][0]), "p": float(t.pvalue),
        })
    out = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    out["p_holm"] = np.nan
    for family, size in FAMILY_SIZES.items():
        m = out["family"] == family
        assert m.sum() == size, f"{family}: {m.sum()} tests, plan says {size}"
        out.loc[m, "p_holm"] = multipletests(out.loc[m, "p"], method="holm")[1]
    out["n"] = int(res.nobs)
    return out


def arm_stats(d, arms, sample):
    g = d.groupby("treatment")["buttonpresses"]
    s = arms[["treatment", "arm"]].copy()
    s["sample"] = sample
    s["n"] = s["treatment"].map(g.size()).astype(int)
    s["mean"] = s["treatment"].map(g.mean())
    s["sd"] = s["treatment"].map(g.std())
    s["se"] = s["sd"] / np.sqrt(s["n"])
    s["ci_low"] = s["mean"] - 1.96 * s["se"]
    s["ci_high"] = s["mean"] + 1.96 * s["se"]
    return s


def figure(stats, path):
    s = stats.iloc[::-1].reset_index(drop=True)  # first arm at the top
    gray, blue, orange, ink = "#8a8984", "#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#0b0b0b"

    def color(t):
        if t in H2_ARMS:
            return blue
        if t == SMALLEST_RATE:
            return orange
        if t == REF:
            return ink
        return gray

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 6.5))
    ref_mean = s.loc[s["treatment"] == REF, "mean"].iloc[0]
    ax.axvline(ref_mean, color=ink, lw=1, ls=(0, (3, 3)), alpha=0.6, zorder=1)
    for i, row in s.iterrows():
        c = color(row["treatment"])
        ax.plot([row["ci_low"], row["ci_high"]], [i, i], color=c, lw=2,
                solid_capstyle="round", zorder=2)
        ax.plot(row["mean"], i, "o", ms=7, color=c, mec="white", mew=1.5, zorder=3)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(s)))
    ax.set_yticklabels([f"{a}  ({t})" for a, t in zip(s["arm"], s["treatment"])], fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_xlabel("Mean points (95% CI)", color="#52514e")
    for side in ["top", "right", "left"]:
        ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines["bottom"].set_color("#c9c8c2")
    ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", colors="#52514e")
    ax.grid(axis="x", color="#ecebe7", lw=0.8, zorder=0)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    handles = [
        plt.Line2D([], [], color=blue, marker="o", lw=2, label="H2: psychological arms (7, 8, 9)"),
        plt.Line2D([], [], color=orange, marker="o", lw=2, label="Arm 2: smallest piece rate"),
        plt.Line2D([], [], color=ink, marker="o", lw=2, label="Arm 1.3: no piece rate (reference, dashed)"),
        plt.Line2D([], [], color=gray, marker="o", lw=2, label="Other arms"),
    ]
    ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.4, 1.0), ncol=2,
              frameon=False, fontsize=8)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(path, dpi=200)
    plt.close(fig)


def main():
    df, arms = load()
    codes = list(arms["treatment"])
    all_tests, all_stats = [], []
    for name, d in samples(df).items():
        res, cols = fit(d, codes)
        all_tests.append(run_tests(res, cols, name))
        all_stats.append(arm_stats(d, arms, name))
    tests = pd.concat(all_tests, ignore_index=True)
    stats = pd.concat(all_stats, ignore_index=True)
    assert (stats.query("sample == 'primary'")["n"].values == arms["clean_n"].values).all()

    tests.to_csv(OUT / "tests.csv", index=False)
    stats.to_csv(OUT / "arm_stats.csv", index=False)
    figure(stats[stats["sample"] == "primary"], OUT / "fig_arm_means.png")

    pd.set_option("display.width", 200)
    for name, t in tests.groupby("sample", sort=False):
        print(f"\n=== {name} (N = {t['n'].iloc[0]:,}) ===")
        show = t[["family", "test", "estimate", "se", "ci_low", "ci_high", "p", "p_holm"]]
        print(show.to_string(index=False, formatters={
            "estimate": "{:.1f}".format, "se": "{:.1f}".format,
            "ci_low": "{:.1f}".format, "ci_high": "{:.1f}".format,
            "p": "{:.4f}".format, "p_holm": "{:.4f}".format}))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

## 1. Introduction

Organizations motivate people with more than pay: reminders of why the work
matters, comparisons with coworkers, rankings, and unexpected gifts meant to
build goodwill. Managers choosing among these tools need to know how much
effort each buys, compared with simply paying a little more per unit of work.
Evidence from separate studies, with different tasks and samples, is hard to
compare on that question.

DellaVigna and Pope (2018) ran a large online experiment that compares 18 ways
of motivating the same dull task within a single design. We reanalyze the raw
data from the authors' replication package for an organizational audience,
asking which motivators raise effort without raising pay, and how they compare
with paying by the piece. Before analyzing outcomes in our data we wrote and froze an
analysis plan, which states three hypotheses:

- **H1.** Paying a piece rate raises effort over paying nothing per unit, and
  a higher piece rate raises it more.
- **H2.** Psychological motivators with no extra pay (social comparison,
  ranking and task significance) raise effort over no piece rate, but less
  than even the smallest piece rate.
- **H3.** An unconditional gift raises effort through reciprocity. This is

## 2. Data and Design

**The experiment.** DellaVigna and Pope (2018) recruited workers on Amazon
Mechanical Turk for a $1 flat fee. In the raw file, start dates run from 15 May
to 5 June 2015; the authors describe the experiment as running "for three weeks
in May 2015" (p. 14). After three demographic questions, workers had 10
minutes to press the "a" and "b" keys alternately as fast as they could, earning one point for each a-b alternation. Each worker
was randomly assigned to one of 18 treatment arms, which differed only in one
paragraph of the task instructions. The study was preregistered on the AEA RCT
Registry (AEARCTR-0000714).[^pages]

[^pages]: Page numbers for DellaVigna and Pope (2018) refer to the NBER
working-paper version (w22193), from which all quotations are taken.

The 18 arms (Table 2) fall into the following groups:
- **Piece rates:** none, or 1, 4 or 10 cents per 100 points.
- **Very low pay:** 1 cent per 1,000 points.
- **Charity:** 1 or 10 cents per 100 points to the Red Cross.
- **Delayed pay:** 1 cent per 100 points, paid in two or four weeks.
- **Threshold bonuses:** 40 cents for 2,000 points or more, framed as a gain
  or as a loss; and 80 cents for 2,000 points or more, framed as a gain.
- **Probabilistic piece rates:** a 1% chance of $1 per 100 points, or a 50%
  chance of 2 cents per 100 points.
- **Gift exchange:** an unconditional bonus of 40 cents.
- **Psychology-based arms:** three arms without pay.

The arms our hypotheses use are worded as follows:

- **Gift exchange:** "In appreciation to you for performing this task, you will
  be paid a bonus of 40 cents. Your score will not affect your payment in any
  way." (DellaVigna and Pope, 2018, p. 8).
- **Social comparison:** "Your score will not affect your payment in any way.
  In a previous version of this task, many participants were able to score
  more than 2,000 points." (DellaVigna and Pope, 2018, p. 52).
- **Ranking:** "Your score will not affect your payment in any way. After you
  play, we will show you how well you did relative to other participants who
  have previously done this task." (DellaVigna and Pope, 2018, p. 52).
- **Task significance:** "Your score will not affect your payment in any way.
  We are interested in how fast people choose to press digits and we would
  like you to do your very best. So please try as hard as you can."
  (DellaVigna and Pope, 2018, p. 11).

DellaVigna and Pope (2018, p. 11) group the last three as their
"psychology-based treatments". They describe ranking as "a second
social-comparison treatment" (p. 11), so H2 covers two kinds of motivator:
social comparison (two arms) and task significance (one arm). Arm 9's wording
asks for effort but does not mention anyone who benefits from the work.
DellaVigna and Pope base the arm on Grant (2008), but we did not check the
original article. We therefore make no claim about how closely the arm
matches Grant (2008).

**Data.** We use the raw data file from the authors' replication package, as
it was before their cleaning and without per-press timestamps. It has one row for
each of the 12,838 workers who started the task, the same initial sample the
authors report (DellaVigna and Pope, 2018, p. 14). It records points scored,
start and end times, completion, bonus paid, practice-round presses, treatment
code and approval status.

**Arm labels.** The file identifies arms by numeric code. We labeled the codes
from a code table in our project notes, which we could not check against the
authors' files. Payouts confirm each code's pay scheme. But four groups of
codes pay identically and cannot be told apart from the data: {1.1, 3.1, 4.1,
4.2}, {1.2, 3.2}, {5.1, 5.2} and {1.3, 7, 8, 9}. Within those groups the
labels rest on the code table.

**Sample.** Table 1 shows how the sample was built, in the order the authors
apply their exclusions (DellaVigna and Pope, 2018, pp. 14–15).

- **Registered exclusions.** We apply the three exclusions in the
  registration, as quoted by DellaVigna and Pope (2018, p. 14):
  - scores of 4,000 points or more, which the registration attributes to bots
    because a pilot showed that more than 3,500 points is "physically
    impossible";
  - not completing the task within 30 minutes of starting, which we apply to
    workers who did not finish or took more than 30 minutes from start to
    end;
  - re-entering the task as a new subject, which we apply to every row of a
    worker ID that appears more than once in the raw file.
- **The authors' added restrictions.** We then apply the two restrictions the

  All 469 rows dropped for having no recorded presses had finished the study
  but have no score.
- **Our own step.** Finally, we drop 4 rows with no treatment code, since
  they cannot be assigned to an arm.

The authors also dropped 721 workers affected by a malfunction of the score
counter when the survey software moved to a new server (p. 14). The raw file

Our final sample has 9,963 workers, 102 (1.0%) more than the authors' 9,861.

Assignment was random at the worker level, so the extra workers should not

## 3. Methods

**Preregistration.** We wrote an analysis plan and attested it on 17 October
2026, before computing any outcome statistic from the data. Until then we had
examined only sample counts, missing values, payout mechanics (to check the
treatment codes) and the cleaning steps. Any deviation from the plan is
reported in Section 5, "Deviations from the plan".

**What was already known.** This is a reanalysis of a published experiment, so
its findings were public before the plan was written. The AI assistant used in
this project (Claude) had also seen some of them before it helped draft the
plan:
- the arm means in DellaVigna and Pope's (2018) Table 4;
- the authors' summary findings, including that the psychological arms were
  less effective than every paid arm.

The hypotheses, arm groupings, comparisons and robustness samples were chosen
by the author. One choice was proposed by the assistant after those findings
were in its context: treating the comparisons of the psychological arms with
the 1-cent piece rate as a separate family for the multiple-comparison
correction.

**Outcome and model.** The outcome is points scored. We estimate one OLS
regression of points on indicators for all 18 arms, with no piece rate (arm
1.3) as the reference and no covariates, and use HC1
heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. Each estimate is a difference in
mean points between two arms:
- a comparison with the no-piece-rate arm is the t-test on that arm's
  coefficient;
- a comparison between two other arms is a test that their two coefficients
  are equal, within the same regression.

All tests are two-sided at α = 0.05.

**Tests.**
- **H1 (6 tests):** each of the 1-, 4- and 10-cent piece rates and the
  very-low-pay arm against no piece rate; and two ordering tests, 10 cents
  against 4 cents and 4 cents against 1 cent.
- **H2 (6 primary tests):** each psychological arm against no piece rate, and
  against the smallest piece rate (1 cent per 1,000 points).
- **H2 secondary (3 tests):** each psychological arm against 1 cent per 100
  points.
- **H3 (1 test):** gift exchange against no piece rate.

The remaining arms are reported descriptively only (Table 2).

**Multiple comparisons.** We apply the Holm correction within each family
(H1, H2 primary, H2 secondary, H3) and report both unadjusted and adjusted
p-values.

**Robustness.** We re-estimate the same tests on two other samples:
- **Complete cases:** workers with no missing points, treatment or
  practice-round count (N = 8,053). Practice counts are missing for 1,910
  workers, so this checks whether results depend on those workers; it is not
  a cleaner sample.
- **Trimmed:** the primary sample with scores above 3,500 removed, the
  registration's threshold for scores impossible by hand (N = 9,950).

These results are reported alongside the primary ones, without separate
inference claims.

**Comparison with the published estimates.** Outside the plan, we compare our
arm means with those reported by DellaVigna and Pope (2018, Table 4) for the
nine arms in our hypotheses. This is a descriptive check only, with no tests.

### 4.1 H1: Piece rates

Every piece rate raised effort over no piece rate:
- 1 cent per 100 points: 507 points (95% CI 426 to 589);
- 4 cents: 606 (526 to 686);
- 10 cents: 649 (572 to 726);
- 1 cent per 1,000 points: 364 (282 to 447).

All four have p < 0.001, unadjusted and Holm-adjusted.

On the ordering, 4 cents raised effort over 1 cent by 99 points (24 to 173;
p = 0.009, Holm p = 0.019). The difference between 10 cents and 4 cents was not
significant: 43 points (−27 to 113; p = 0.226, Holm p = 0.226).

H1 is supported for paying something over paying nothing. Its claim that a
higher piece rate raises effort more is supported from 1 cent to 4 cents but
not from 4 cents to 10 cents.

### 4.2 H2: Psychological motivators

Each psychological arm raised effort over no piece rate:
- social comparison (arm 7): 334 points (247 to 421);
- ranking (arm 8): 234 (148 to 320);
- task significance (arm 9): 215 (132 to 298).

All three have p < 0.001, unadjusted and Holm-adjusted.

Against the smallest piece rate (arm 2, 1 cent per 1,000 points), ranking and
task significance raised effort less:
- ranking: −130 points (−212 to −48; p = 0.002, Holm p = 0.004);
- task significance: −149 points (−228 to −70; p < 0.001, Holm p < 0.001).

Social comparison raised points relative to no piece rate by 334 (95% CI 247
to 421). Its difference from the smallest piece rate was −30 points (95% CI
−114 to +54; Holm-adjusted p = 0.48). The data therefore neither show that
social comparison is less effective than the smallest piece rate nor that it
is as effective. They are consistent with a shortfall of up to about 114
points, or an advantage of up to about 54. For arm 7, the "less than even the
smallest piece rate" part of H2 is inconclusive. It is supported for ranking
(arm 8) and task significance (arm 9).

In the secondary family, all three psychological arms fell short of 1 cent
per 100 points (all p < 0.001, unadjusted and Holm-adjusted):
- social comparison: −173 (−256 to −91);
- ranking: −273 (−354 to −193);
- task significance: −293 (−370 to −215).

### 4.3 H3: Gift exchange

The unconditional 40-cent gift raised points over no piece rate by 72 (95% CI
−13 to 156; p = 0.095). With a single test in the family, the Holm p-value is
the same. The difference is not significant. The interval includes zero, and
also includes gains of up to about 156 points.

## 6. Comparison with the published estimates (unplanned)

As a descriptive check outside the plan, we compared our arm means with those
reported in DellaVigna and Pope (2018, Table 4) for the nine arms in our
hypotheses.
- **Arm means:** ours are within 11 points of theirs.
- **Gaps from no piece rate:** ours are within 10 points of theirs. The
  largest differences are for gift exchange (−9) and social comparison (+7),
  both small next to standard errors of about 43 points.

The extra 102 workers in our sample therefore do not appear to change the
comparisons between arms materially. The match also supports the labels for
the codes it covers, which the payouts could not settle. Arm 7, for example,
matches the published social-comparison mean, not the no-piece-rate mean. The
check has two limits:
- it cannot tell ranking from task significance, whose published means differ
  by only 21 points;
- it does not cover the charity, delayed-pay and threshold codes.

## 7. Discussion

These results come from one dull, 10-minute key-pressing task done by
Mechanical Turk workers for a $1 fee. They show how the motivators compare in
that setting. They cannot tell us whether the same pattern holds for other
tasks, longer jobs or real workplaces.

**Pay (H1).** Every piece rate raised effort over paying nothing per unit,
including 1 cent per 1,000 points. Raising the rate from 1 to 4 cents per 100
points added effort, but we could not distinguish 10 cents from 4 cents. In
this task, the move from no piece rate to some piece rate did the most work.
Beyond a modest rate, the data do not show further gains.

**Motivators without extra pay (H2).** Social comparison, ranking and the
task-significance message each raised effort over no piece rate, so in this
setting some extra effort came without extra pay per unit. All three fell
short of 1 cent per 100 points. Ranking and task significance also fell short
of the smallest piece rate, though in one robustness sample the ranking
shortfall was not significant after correction. For social comparison, the
comparison with the smallest piece rate is inconclusive: the data neither
show that social comparison is less effective than a token piece rate, nor
that it is as effective.

**Gift (H3).** The unconditional 40-cent gift did not raise effort
significantly. Its confidence interval includes zero as well as modest gains,
so the data neither show that the gift worked nor rule out a small effect. In
this task, nothing here suggests that a gift substitutes for paying by the
piece.

# What Motivates Effort on Dull Work? A Preregistered Reanalysis of DellaVigna and Pope (2018)

## Abstract

We reanalyze an online experiment by DellaVigna and Pope (2018) in which
Mechanical Turk workers were randomly assigned to one of 18 ways of motivating
a dull, 10-minute key-pressing task. Our sample has 9,963 workers, against the
authors' 9,861, because one of their exclusions cannot be reproduced from the
raw data. Every piece rate raised effort over no piece rate, including 1 cent
per 1,000 points. Paying 4 cents per 100 points raised effort over 1 cent, but
10 cents could not be distinguished from 4 cents. Social comparison, ranking
and a task-significance message each raised effort over no piece rate, but all
three fell short of 1 cent per 100 points. Ranking and task significance also
fell short of the smallest piece rate. For social comparison, that comparison
is inconclusive. An unconditional 40-cent gift did not raise effort
significantly. Our tests follow a preregistered plan, but the plan was written
after the published results were public.

## 1. Introduction

Organizations motivate people with more than pay: reminders of why the work
matters, comparisons with coworkers, rankings, and unexpected gifts meant to
build goodwill. Managers choosing among these tools need to know how much
effort each buys, compared with simply paying a little more per unit of work.
As DellaVigna and Pope (2018, p. 1) note, "Different dependent variables and
dissimilar participant samples can make direct comparisons of effect sizes
across various studies difficult."

DellaVigna and Pope (2018) ran a large online experiment that compares 18 ways
of motivating the same dull task within a single design. We reanalyze the raw
data from the authors' replication package for an organizational audience,
asking which motivators raise effort without raising pay, and how they compare
with paying by the piece. Before analyzing outcomes in our data we wrote and froze an
analysis plan, which states three hypotheses:

- **H1.** Paying a piece rate raises effort over paying nothing per unit, and
  a higher piece rate raises it more.
- **H2.** Psychological motivators with no extra pay (social comparison,
  ranking and task significance) raise effort over no piece rate, but less
  than even the smallest piece rate.
- **H3.** An unconditional gift raises effort through reciprocity. This is
  the plan's hypothesis, stated without a supporting citation.

Two of the arms draw on earlier work, as DellaVigna and Pope describe it.
They design their very-low-pay arm "as in Gneezy and Rustichini (2000)"
(DellaVigna and Pope, 2018, p. 7). Their task-significance arm "is based on
the influential literature in psychology on task significance (Grant, 2008)"
(DellaVigna and Pope, 2018, p. 11). We cite these two works only for how
DellaVigna and Pope used them. We did not check the original articles, and
we make no claim about what either one found or how it defines its terms.

Section 7 (Contribution) sets out what this reanalysis adds.

## 2. Data and Design

**The experiment.** DellaVigna and Pope (2018) recruited workers on Amazon
Mechanical Turk for a $1 flat fee. In the raw file, start dates run from 15 May
to 5 June 2015; the authors describe the experiment as running "for three weeks
in May 2015" (p. 14). After three demographic questions, workers had 10
minutes to press the "a" and "b" keys alternately as fast as they could,
earning one point for each a-b alternation. Each worker was randomly assigned
to one of 18 treatment arms, which differed only in one paragraph of the task
instructions. The study was preregistered on the AEA RCT Registry (AEARCTR-0000714).[^pages]

[^pages]: Page numbers for DellaVigna and Pope (2018) refer to the NBER
working-paper version (w22193), from which all quotations are taken.

Table A1 (Appendix) lists all 18 arms. The arms our hypotheses use are worded as follows:

- **Gift exchange:** "In appreciation to you for performing this task, you will
  be paid a bonus of 40 cents. Your score will not affect your payment in any
  way." (DellaVigna and Pope, 2018, p. 8).
- **Social comparison:** "Your score will not affect your payment in any way.
  In a previous version of this task, many participants were able to score
  more than 2,000 points." (DellaVigna and Pope, 2018, p. 52).
- **Ranking:** "Your score will not affect your payment in any way. After you
  play, we will show you how well you did relative to other participants who
  have previously done this task." (DellaVigna and Pope, 2018, p. 52).
- **Task significance:** "Your score will not affect your payment in any way.
  We are interested in how fast people choose to press digits and we would
  like you to do your very best. So please try as hard as you can."
  (DellaVigna and Pope, 2018, p. 11).

DellaVigna and Pope (2018, p. 11) group the last three as their
"psychology-based treatments". They describe ranking as "a second
social-comparison treatment" (p. 11), so H2 covers two kinds of motivator:
social comparison (two arms) and task significance (one arm). Arm 9's wording
asks for effort but does not mention anyone who benefits from the work.
DellaVigna and Pope base the arm on Grant (2008), but we did not check the
original article. We therefore make no claim about how closely the arm
matches Grant (2008).

**Data.** We use the raw data file from the authors' replication package, as
it was before their cleaning and without per-press timestamps. It has one row
for each of the 12,838 workers who started the task, the same initial sample the
authors report (DellaVigna and Pope, 2018, p. 14). It records points scored,
start and end times, completion, bonus paid, practice-round presses, treatment
code and approval status.

**Arm labels.** The file identifies arms by numeric code. We labeled the codes
from a code table in our project notes, which we could not check against the
authors' files. Payouts confirm each code's pay scheme. But four groups of
codes pay identically and cannot be told apart from the data: {1.1, 3.1, 4.1,
4.2}, {1.2, 3.2}, {5.1, 5.2} and {1.3, 7, 8, 9}. Within those groups the
labels rest on the code table.

**Sample.** Table 1 shows how the sample was built, in the order the authors
apply their exclusions (DellaVigna and Pope, 2018, pp. 14–15).

We apply the three exclusions in the registration, as quoted by DellaVigna
and Pope (2018, p. 14), then the two restrictions the authors added (p. 15),
and finally drop rows with no treatment code, which cannot be assigned to an
arm. The registration excludes scores of 4,000 points or more as likely bots,
because a pilot showed that more than 3,500 points is "physically
impossible". The notes to Table 1 give our operational definitions.

The authors also dropped 721 workers affected by a malfunction of the score
counter when the survey software moved to a new server (p. 14). The raw file
does not flag these workers, and the paper gives no time window, so we do not
reconstruct this exclusion.

Our final sample has 9,963 workers, 102 (1.0%) more than the authors' 9,861.
The difference is spread evenly across arms: each has 0 to 9 more workers than
the authors report (532–577 per arm, against their "about 550"; p. 15).
Section 6 compares our arm means with the published ones.

## 3. Methods

**Preregistration.** We wrote an analysis plan and attested it on 17 October
2026, before computing any outcome statistic from the data. Until then we had
examined only sample counts, missing values, payout mechanics (to check the
treatment codes) and the cleaning steps. Any deviation from the plan is
reported in Section 5, "Deviations from the plan".

**What was already known.** This is a reanalysis of a published experiment, so
its findings were public before the plan was written. The AI assistant used in
this project (Claude) had seen DellaVigna and Pope's (2018) arm means and
summary findings before it helped draft the plan. The author chose the
hypotheses, comparisons and robustness samples; after seeing those findings,
the assistant proposed treating the comparisons with the 1-cent piece rate as
a separate multiple-comparison family.

**Outcome and model.** The outcome is points scored. We estimate one OLS
regression of points on indicators for all 18 arms, with no piece rate (arm
1.3) as the reference and no covariates, and use HC1
heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. Each estimate is a difference in
mean points between two arms:
- a comparison with the no-piece-rate arm is the t-test on that arm's
  coefficient;
- a comparison between two other arms is a test that their two coefficients
  are equal, within the same regression.

All tests are two-sided at α = 0.05.

**Tests.** H1 compares each piece rate, including 1 cent per 1,000 points,
with no piece rate and tests two orderings (10 against 4 cents, 4 against 1
cent); H2 compares each psychological arm with no piece rate and with the
smallest piece rate (primary family) and with 1 cent per 100 points (secondary
family); H3 compares gift exchange with no piece rate. Table 2 lists all 16
tests by family, and the remaining arms are reported descriptively only
(Table A1, Appendix).

**Multiple comparisons.** We apply the Holm correction within each family
(H1, H2 primary, H2 secondary, H3) and report both unadjusted and adjusted
p-values.

**Robustness.** We re-estimate the same tests on two other samples:
- **Complete cases:** workers with no missing points, treatment or
  practice-round count (N = 8,053). Practice counts are missing for 1,910
  workers, so this checks whether results depend on those workers; it is not
  a cleaner sample.
- **Trimmed:** the primary sample with scores above 3,500 removed, the
  registration's threshold for scores impossible by hand (N = 9,950).

These results are reported alongside the primary ones, without separate
inference claims.

**Comparison with the published estimates.** Outside the plan, we compare our
arm means with those reported by DellaVigna and Pope (2018, Table 4) for the
nine arms in our hypotheses. This is a descriptive check only, with no tests.

### 4.1 H1: Piece rates

Every piece rate raised effort over no piece rate, including 1 cent per
1,000 points (Table 2; all four p < 0.001, unadjusted and Holm-adjusted).

On the ordering, 4 cents raised effort over 1 cent by 99 points (24 to 173;
p = 0.009, Holm p = 0.019). The difference between 10 cents and 4 cents was not
significant: 43 points (−27 to 113; p = 0.226, Holm p = 0.226).

H1 is supported for paying something over paying nothing. Its claim that a
higher piece rate raises effort more is supported from 1 cent to 4 cents but
not from 4 cents to 10 cents.

### 4.2 H2: Psychological motivators

Each psychological arm raised effort over no piece rate (Table 2; all three
p < 0.001, unadjusted and Holm-adjusted). Against the smallest piece rate (arm
2, 1 cent per 1,000 points), ranking and task significance raised effort less
(Holm p = 0.004 and Holm p < 0.001).

Social comparison raised points relative to no piece rate by 334 (95% CI 247
to 421). Its difference from the smallest piece rate was −30 points (95% CI
−114 to +54; Holm-adjusted p = 0.48). The data therefore neither show that
social comparison is less effective than the smallest piece rate nor that it
is as effective. They are consistent with a shortfall of up to about 114
points, or an advantage of up to about 54. For arm 7, the "less than even the
smallest piece rate" part of H2 is inconclusive. It is supported for ranking
(arm 8) and task significance (arm 9).

In the secondary family, all three psychological arms fell short of 1 cent
per 100 points (Table 2; all p < 0.001, unadjusted and Holm-adjusted).

### 4.3 H3: Gift exchange

The unconditional 40-cent gift raised points over no piece rate by 72 (95% CI
−13 to 156; p = 0.095). With a single test in the family, the Holm p-value is
the same. The difference is not significant. The interval includes zero, and
also includes gains of up to about 156 points.

As a descriptive check outside the plan, we compared our arm means with those

- **Arm means:** ours are within 11 points of theirs.
- **Gaps from no piece rate:** ours are within 10 points of theirs. The

- it does not cover the charity, delayed-pay and threshold codes.

## 7. Discussion

These results come from one dull, 10-minute key-pressing task done by
Mechanical Turk workers for a $1 fee. They show how the motivators compare in
that setting. They cannot tell us whether the same pattern holds for other
tasks, longer jobs or real workplaces.

**Pay (H1).** Every piece rate raised effort over paying nothing per unit,
including 1 cent per 1,000 points. Raising the rate from 1 to 4 cents per 100
points added effort, but we could not distinguish 10 cents from 4 cents. H1 is
supported for paying something over paying nothing; its ordering is supported
from 1 cent to 4 cents but not from 4 cents to 10 cents.

**Motivators without extra pay (H2).** Social comparison, ranking and the
task-significance message each raised effort over no piece rate, so in this
setting some extra effort came without extra pay per unit. All three fell
short of 1 cent per 100 points. Ranking and task significance also fell short
of the smallest piece rate, though in one robustness sample the ranking
shortfall was not significant after correction. For social comparison, the
comparison with the smallest piece rate is inconclusive: the data neither
show that social comparison is less effective than a token piece rate, nor
that it is as effective.

**Gift (H3).** The unconditional 40-cent gift did not raise effort
significantly (95% CI −13 to 156 points). Its confidence interval includes zero as well as modest gains,
so the data neither show that the gift worked nor rule out a small effect.

### Contribution

<!-- BEGIN contribution -->
This paper adds a managerial reading to a data set that was built for economists. In one design, with one task and one pool of workers, it puts the common non-pay motivators (social comparison, ranking, a plain appeal to effort) next to piece rates of several sizes and to an unconditional gift. For an organizational audience, the useful result is a ranking within that design. Each of the three no-pay messages raised effort over paying nothing per unit, but all of them fell short of a 1-cent-per-100-points piece rate, and ranking and the task-significance message also fell short of a piece rate of 1 cent per 1,000 points. The unconditional gift did not raise effort by a margin we can distinguish from zero. A manager weighing a message against a small payment can therefore see how much effort the message bought here, and where it stopped. I do not claim that the same ordering holds for other tasks, longer jobs, or workers who stay with an employer, nor that the task-significance arm tests the construct as the organizational literature defines it. I did not check that literature against the original articles for this paper.
<!-- END contribution -->

### Limitations

<!-- BEGIN limitations -->
First, this is one task: pressing two keys for ten minutes, for a $1 fee, done by online workers who had no relationship with the requester. Motivation in a workplace with colleagues, a manager and a future with the employer may work very differently, and so may the value of a message or a gift. Second, our sample is not the authors' sample. We end with 9,963 workers against their 9,861, because the raw file does not identify the 721 workers they dropped for a server malfunction, and some of our extra workers may have mismeasured scores. Our arm means are close to the published ones, but this does not show that the samples are the same. Third, the arm labels for four groups of codes rest on our notes, since payouts cannot separate them, and the check against the published means cannot tell ranking from task significance. Fourth, arm 9's wording does not mention who benefits from the work, and I did not read Grant (2008), so I cannot say how well it tests task significance. Fifth, the plan was written after the published results were public, and our assistant had seen some of them. The tests are preregistered in our sense only. Sixth, the analysis is confined to total points. It says nothing about work quality, later effort, or whether a message loses its effect when it is repeated. Seventh, the inconclusive result for social comparison against the smallest piece rate, and the non-significant gift effect, are not evidence of equivalence or of no effect.
